column2: Same brand. Same menu. Same opening hours, at every site. But the people outside site one aren't the people outside site ten.

Wendell Smith named market segmentation in nineteen fifty-six. Marketing courses now teach it as three steps: segment the market, choose a target, then position yourself for it. Multi-site owners usually do it once, for the brand. Do it again for every site.

Site one sits by a station. Its guests arrive between seven and nine, in a hurry, and spend six pounds each. Site ten sits on a residential street. Its busiest hours are weekend late mornings, with guests who stay.

But site ten runs site one's menu: a coffee and a pastry, to go. On a Saturday, two hundred guests spend seven pounds each. Give them a brunch worth eleven pounds a head, and the same guests add eight hundred pounds a week. Enough to take site ten past break-even.
That's positioning. Same brand, same name above the door. But the menu, the hours and the rota at each site are set for the guests on its own street.
Your question for Monday: who is each of your sites actually for?
